lessons.title: Magnetic fields and forces on moving charges
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — magnetic fields and electromagnetic induction (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Use F = BIl sin θ and F = Bqv sin θ with Fleming's left-hand rule
Analyse a charged particle moving in a uniform magnetic field (r = mv/qB) and describe the velocity selector and mass spectrometer
Calculate the magnetic field of a long wire and a solenoid and the force between parallel currents
reviewNotes: Constants used: e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s; mₑ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg; ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m; μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ H/m.
Hall effect and the cyclotron are not covered; check the syllabus.
Fleming's rules are described in words; the direction conventions should be checked against the board's preferred rule (left-hand/right-hand).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Magnetic flux density and forces
blocks.md:
The **magnetic flux density** B (tesla, T = N A⁻¹ m⁻¹) is defined by the force on a current-carrying conductor perpendicular to the field: **F = BIl** (in general F = BIl sin θ, θ = angle between the wire and B).

On a moving charge: **F = Bqv sin θ**, always perpendicular to both v and B (Fleming's left-hand rule for a positive charge: first finger field, second finger current/velocity, thumb force). The force does **no work**, so the speed is unchanged.

blocks.title: Motion in a uniform field
blocks.md:
A charge entering a uniform field at right angles moves on a **circle**: Bqv = mv²/r gives **r = mv/(qB)**, with period **T = 2πm/(qB)** independent of the speed.

**Velocity selector**: crossed fields E and B; particles with v = E/B pass undeflected. **Mass spectrometer**: ions accelerated through V (qV = ½mv²) move on a circle of radius r = (1/B)√(2mV/q), so r depends on the mass.

blocks.caption: A charged particle moving at right angles to a field into the page: the force is perpendicular to the velocity, so the path is a circle.
blocks.alt: A grid of crosses showing a magnetic field into the page, a circular path with a velocity arrow along the tangent and a force arrow to the centre.

blocks.title: Fields of currents
blocks.md:
Long straight wire: **B = μ₀I/(2πr)** (direction by the right-hand grip rule). Long solenoid with n turns per metre: **B = μ₀nI** inside, almost zero outside. μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹.

Two long parallel wires carrying I₁ and I₂ at distance d attract if the currents are in the same direction: **F/L = μ₀I₁I₂/(2πd)**. This defines the ampere (2 × 10⁻⁷ N m⁻¹ for 1 A in wires 1 m apart).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the wrong hand: the left-hand rule is for the force on a conductor (motor effect); the right-hand rule is used for the field of a current.
- Forgetting that the force on a negative charge is opposite to the left-hand rule direction.
- Using θ as the angle to the perpendicular: it is between the field and the wire or velocity.
- Believing the magnetic force changes the speed: it only changes the direction.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Wire in a field
blocks.statement: A straight wire 0.25 m long carries 8.0 A at right angles to a field of 0.40 T. Find the force. Then find B at 5.0 cm from a long straight wire carrying 10 A.
steps: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10 ÷ (2π × 0.050) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁵ T (comparable with the Earth's field).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Electron in a field
blocks.statement: An electron moves at 2.0 × 10⁷ m/s at right angles to a field of 1.0 mT. Find the radius and period of its circular path.

lessons.title: Electromagnetic induction
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — magnetic fields and electromagnetic induction (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define magnetic flux and flux linkage and state Faraday's and Lenz's laws
Calculate the emf induced in a moving conductor (ε = Blv), a changing field and a rotating coil
Explain eddy currents and the operation of a simple a.c. generator
reviewNotes: Self-inductance and energy stored in an inductor are not covered; check the syllabus.
Direction rules (Fleming's right-hand rule) are described through Lenz's law only.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Flux and the laws of induction
blocks.md:
**Magnetic flux** Φ = BA cos θ (weber, Wb = T m²) where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the area. **Flux linkage** = NΦ for a coil of N turns.

**Faraday's law**: the induced emf equals the rate of change of flux linkage: **ε = −N ΔΦ/Δt**. **Lenz's law** (the minus sign): the induced current flows in a direction that opposes the change producing it (conservation of energy).

blocks.title: Useful results
blocks.md:
- Straight conductor of length l moving at speed v at right angles to B: **ε = Blv**.
- Coil of N turns, area A, rotating at angular speed ω in field B: **ε = NBAω sin ωt**, so the peak emf is ε₀ = NBAω.
- Eddy currents: induced currents in a bulk conductor that oppose the motion (used in induction cookers and electromagnetic braking, and reduced by laminating transformer cores).

blocks.caption: A rod sliding on rails in a field into the page: emf = Blv.
blocks.alt: Two horizontal rails joined at the left, a vertical rod moving to the right, crosses showing a field into the page and the emf formula.

blocks.title: Direction and energy
blocks.md:
If a magnet is pushed towards a coil, the coil end nearest the magnet becomes the same pole as the approaching pole, repelling it: work must be done to push it, and that work becomes electrical energy. If Lenz's law were reversed, energy would be created from nothing.

For a moving rod: electrical power εI = mechanical power Fv.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Thinking an emf is induced by a steady flux: only a **change** of flux induces an emf.
- Forgetting N, the number of turns, in Faraday's law.
- Treating the minus sign as meaning a negative emf rather than 'opposing the change'.
- Mixing flux (Wb) with flux density (T).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Moving rod
blocks.statement: A rod 0.50 m long moves at 4.0 m/s at right angles to a field of 0.30 T on rails joined to a 2.0 Ω resistor. Find the emf, the current, the magnetic force on the rod and the power.
steps: Force F = BIl = 0.30 × 0.30 × 0.50 = 0.045 N, opposing the motion.
Power = Fv = 0.045 × 4.0 = 0.18 W = εI ✓ (the energy comes from whoever pushes the rod).

blocks.title: Example 2 — Changing field
blocks.statement: A coil of 200 turns and area 1.0 × 10⁻² m² has its axis along a field that falls from 0.50 T to zero in 0.020 s. Find the average emf.
steps: Change of flux = ΔB × A = 0.50 × 1.0 × 10⁻² = 5.0 × 10⁻³ Wb.

lessons.title: Alternating current and transformers
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — magnetic fields and electromagnetic induction (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe a sinusoidal alternating current and use peak, r.m.s. values, frequency and period
Use P = I_rms V_rms and the transformer equation V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p; explain high-voltage power transmission
Describe half-wave and full-wave rectification, and the reactance of a capacitor
reviewNotes: Mains in Cameroon: 220 V (r.m.s.) and 50 Hz assumed; to be confirmed.
Reactance, impedance of RLC circuits and resonance are only touched (capacitor reactance); check the syllabus before extending.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Alternating current and r.m.s. values
blocks.md:
An alternating current varies sinusoidally: **I = I₀ sin ωt**, **V = V₀ sin ωt** with ω = 2πf. The **r.m.s.** (root mean square) value is the steady d.c. value that would dissipate the same power in a resistor:

**I_rms = I₀/√2**, **V_rms = V₀/√2**. Mean power P = I_rms V_rms = ½I₀V₀ = I_rms²R.

blocks.title: Transformers
blocks.md:
A transformer works by mutual induction in two coils on a soft-iron core and needs a.c. For an ideal transformer: **V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p** and (100 % efficient) V_pI_p = V_sI_s, so a step-up transformer gives a smaller current.

Real transformers lose energy by resistance of the coils (heating), eddy currents, hysteresis and flux leakage; efficiency = P_out/P_in × 100 %.

blocks.caption: A sinusoidal alternating voltage: the r.m.s. value is 0.707 of the peak.
blocks.alt: A sine wave over two periods with a dashed horizontal line at 0.707 of the peak value.

blocks.title: Power transmission and rectification
blocks.md:
Electricity is transmitted at high voltage and low current to reduce the power lost in the cables (P_loss = I²R). A **diode** conducts in one direction only: **half-wave rectification** removes half the cycle; four diodes in a bridge give **full-wave rectification**; a smoothing capacitor reduces the ripple.

The **reactance** of a capacitor to a.c. is X_C = 1/(2πfC): it falls with frequency (blocks d.c.).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Quoting mains as 220 V peak: 220 V is the r.m.s. value; the peak is about 311 V.
- Using the peak value in P = V²/R: use r.m.s.
- Believing a transformer works on d.c. (a steady current gives no changing flux).
- Forgetting that a step-up transformer does not give more power: it steps down the current.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Peak and r.m.s.
blocks.statement: A mains supply is rated 220 V (r.m.s.), 50 Hz. Find the peak voltage, the period, and the mean power in a 44 Ω heater.
blocks.answer: V₀ = 311 V; T = 20 ms; P = 1.1 kW

blocks.title: Example 2 — Transformer and transmission
blocks.statement: (a) A transformer has 1100 turns on the primary (220 V). How many secondary turns give 12 V? (b) A 100 kW supply is sent along cables of total resistance 5.0 Ω at 10 kV, and at 1.0 kV. Find the power loss.
steps: At 1.0 kV: I = 100 A, loss = 100² × 5.0 = 50 000 W (half the power!). High voltage wastes far less.
